title: Written Stories Have Lasted Thousands of Years. A Generation Raised on Screens Needs to Be Shown Why They’re Worth the Effort.
author: Jennifer Haber
summary: Jennifer Haber, a middle school English teacher of thirty years, argues that teachers can no longer assume seventh graders know what it feels like to get lost in a book, because screens now offer endless effortless stories. Her answer is a three-part strategy for making reading feel worth the effort. First she explains the science, citing studies showing that reading activates the same brain regions used for real experience and that curiosity enhances memory. Second she turns content into a mystery, such as asking how stories thousands of years apart share the same themes. Third she reads whole novels aloud and lets students see her genuinely moved. She anchors the year in the Epic of Gilgamesh and concludes that stories will survive a screen generation because being human has hardly changed.
points: Haber frames the central challenge as persuading students that reading is worth the effort, since a screen competes with every book and offers stories that demand no imagination.

She uses cognitive science (brain responses to narrative and the reward circuitry of curiosity) as a student-facing argument, not just teacher background, explaining that reading makes the reader build the story while film hands it over.
Phrasing a statement as a mystery, such as how distant cultures produce the same themes, turns information into a question students want solved and makes engagement simpler than games or videos.
Reading whole books aloud, and letting students see the teacher visibly moved by a scene, shows rather than tells what absorption in a story looks like.
Starting the year with the Epic of Gilgamesh makes the argument concrete, because students find friendship, grief and guilt as real today as four thousand years ago.
quotes: As we all know, that isn’t enough anymore. My students have a screen in their pockets that can give them something new to watch almost endlessly.
Reading takes more patience than that, especially at the beginning, because they have to build so much of the story in their own minds before they know whether they are going to care about it.
When you watch a movie, someone else has already made many of those choices for you. You don’t get to decide what a character looks like or sounds like.
When I pose the same idea as a mystery to solve, they get curious, and curiosity is what makes them want to explore further.
I read whole books aloud to my class rather than assigning chapters to be read at home, and I’ve written about why in a separate article called Yes, I Read the Whole Novel to My Seventh Graders.
Every time I read it, I tear up, and I don’t hide it from my students. I’ve read that scene more times than I can count, and it still gets me.
Human life has changed enormously since Gilgamesh, but being human has hardly changed at all.
Screens have changed almost everything about how my students spend their time, but they haven’t changed what it means to be human.
